{{Short description|Abelian group}}
In [[arithmetic geometry]], the '''Mordell–Weil group''' is an [[abelian group]] associated to any [[abelian variety]] <math>A</math> defined over a number field <math>K</math>. It is an arithmetic invariant of the Abelian variety. It is simply the group of <math>K</math>-points of <math>A</math>, so <math>A(K)</math> is the Mordell–Weil group<ref>{{Cite journal|last=Tate|first=John T.|author-link=John Tate (mathematician)|date=1974-09-01|title=The arithmetic of elliptic curves|url=https://doi.org/10.1007/BF01389745|journal=Inventiones Mathematicae|language=en|volume=23|issue=3|pages=179–206|doi=10.1007/BF01389745|bibcode=1974InMat..23..179T |s2cid=120008651 |issn=1432-1297|url-access=subscription}}</ref><ref>{{Cite book|last=Silverman, Joseph H.|author-link=Joseph H. Silverman|title=The arithmetic of elliptic curves|date=2009|publisher=Springer-Verlag|isbn=978-0-387-09494-6|edition=2nd|location=New York|pages=|oclc=405546184}}</ref><sup>pg 207</sup>. The main structure theorem about this group is the [[Mordell–Weil theorem]] which shows this group is in fact a finitely-generated abelian group. Moreover, there are many conjectures related to this group, such as the [[Birch and Swinnerton-Dyer conjecture]] which relates the [[Rank of an abelian group|rank]] of <math>A(K)</math> to the zero of the associated [[L-function]] at a special point.

== Examples ==
Constructing explicit examples of the Mordell–Weil group of an abelian variety is a non-trivial process which is not always guaranteed to be successful,<ref name=":0" /> so we instead specialize to the case of a specific [[elliptic curve]] <math>E/\mathbb{Q}</math>. Let <math>E</math> be defined by the [[Cubic plane curve#Weierstrass normal form|Weierstrass equation]]
:<math>y^2 = x(x-6)(x+6)</math>
over the rational numbers. It has discriminant <math>\Delta_E = 2^{12}\cdot 3^6</math> (and this polynomial can be used to define a global model <math>\mathcal{E}/\mathbb{Z}</math>). It can be found that<ref name=":0">{{Cite web|last=Booher|first=Jeremy|date=|title=The Mordell–Weil theorem for elliptic curves|url=https://www.math.arizona.edu/~jeremybooher/expos/mordellweil.pdf|url-status=live|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210127183440/https://www.math.arizona.edu/~jeremybooher/expos/mordellweil.pdf|archive-date=27 Jan 2021|access-date=|website=}}</ref>
:<math>E(\mathbb{Q}) \cong \mathbb{Z}/2\times \mathbb{Z}/2 \times \mathbb{Z}</math>
through the following procedure: first, we find [[torsion subgroup|torsion points]] by plugging in some numbers, which are
:<math>\infty, (0,0), (6,0), (-6,0).</math>
In addition, after trying some smaller pairs of integers, we find <math>(-3,9)</math> is a point which is not obviously torsion. One useful result for finding the torsion part of <math>E(\mathbb{Q})</math> is that the torsion of prime to <math>p</math>, for <math>E</math> having [[good reduction]] to <math>p</math>, denoted <math>E(\mathbb{Q})_{\mathrm{tors},p}</math> injects into <math>E(\mathbb{F}_p)</math>. We check at two primes <math>p = 5,7</math> and calculate the cardinality of the sets
:<math>\begin{align}
\# E(\mathbb{F}_5) &= 8 = 2^3 \\
\# E(\mathbb{F}_{7}) &= 12 = 2^2\cdot 3 
\end{align}</math>
Note that because both primes only contain a common factor of <math>2^2</math>, we have found all the torsion points. In addition, we know the point <math>(-3,9)</math> has infinite order because otherwise there would be a prime factor shared by both cardinalities, so the [[Rank of an elliptic curve|rank]] is at least <math>1</math>. Now, computing the rank is a more arduous process consisting of calculating the group <math>E(\mathbb{Q})/2E(\mathbb{Q}) \cong (\mathbb{Z}/2)^{r + 2}</math> where <math>r = \operatorname{rank}(E(\mathbb{Q}))</math> using some long exact sequences from [[homological algebra]] and the [[Kummer theory#The Kummer Map|Kummer map]].

== Theorems concerning special cases ==
There are many theorems in the literature about the structure of the Mordell–Weil groups of abelian varieties of specific dimension, over specific fields, or having some other special property.

=== Abelian varieties over the rational function field ''k''(''t'') ===
For a [[hyperelliptic curve]] <math>C</math> and an abelian variety <math>A</math> defined over a fixed field <math>k</math>, we denote the <math>A_b</math> the twist of <math>A|_{k(t)}</math> (the pullback of <math>A</math> to the function field <math>k(t) = k(\mathbb{P}^1)</math>) by a 1-cocyle<blockquote><math>b \in Z^1(\operatorname{Gal}(k(C)/k(t)), \text{Aut}(A))</math></blockquote>for [[Galois cohomology]] of the [[field extension]] associated to the covering map <math>f:C \to \mathbb{P}^1</math>. Note <math>G = \operatorname{Gal}(k(C)/k(t) \cong \mathbb{Z}/2</math> which follows from the map being hyperelliptic. More explicitly, this 1-cocyle is given as a map of groups<blockquote><math>G\times G \to \operatorname{Aut}(A)</math></blockquote>which using [[Universal property|universal properties]] is the same as giving two maps <math>G \to \text{Aut}(A)</math>, hence we can write it as a map<blockquote><math>b = (b_{id}, b_{\iota})</math></blockquote>where <math>b_{id}</math> is the [[inclusion map]] and <math>b_\iota</math> is sent to negative <math>\operatorname{Id}_A</math>. This can be used to define the [[twisted abelian variety]] <math>A_b</math> defined over <math>k(t)</math> using general theory of algebraic geometry<ref>{{Cite book|last=Weil, André, 1906-1998.|title=Adeles and algebraic groups|date=1982|publisher=Birkhäuser|isbn=978-1-4684-9156-2|location=Boston|pages=|chapter=1.3|oclc=681203844}}</ref><sup>pg 5</sup>. In particular, from universal properties of this construction, <math>A_b</math> is an abelian variety over <math>k(t)</math> which is isomorphic to <math>A|_{k(C)}</math> after base-change to <math>k(C)</math>.

==== Theorem ====
For the setup given above,<ref>{{Cite journal|last=Hazama|first=Fumio|date=1992|title=The Mordell–Weil group of certain abelian varieties defined over the rational function field|url=https://projecteuclid.org/euclid.tmj/1178227300|journal=Tohoku Mathematical Journal|language=EN|volume=44|issue=3|pages=335–344|doi=10.2748/tmj/1178227300|issn=0040-8735|doi-access=free}}</ref> there is an isomorphism of abelian groups<blockquote><math>A_b(k(t)) \cong \operatorname{Hom}_k(J(C), A)\oplus A_2(k)</math></blockquote>where <math>J(C)</math> is the Jacobian of the curve <math>C</math>, and <math>A_2</math> is the 2-torsion subgroup of <math>A</math>.
